los.text: Describe the importance of safeguarding and child protection (and consequences of failures to do so)
sessions: Case presentation and Introduction to Safeguarding Children
los.html:
Safeguarding
  • Protecting children from maltreatment, preventing impairment of health/development, ensuring safe and effective care, enabling best outcomes.
  • Child protection = part of safeguarding: action for children suffering or at risk of significant harm.
Why it matters
  • Common: ~1 in 5 adults report childhood abuse.
  • Causes death and lifelong harm (mental illness, substance misuse, chronic disease: ACEs).
  • Often missed at first presentation (sentinel injuries).
Consequences of failure
  • Preventable deaths and serious harm.
  • Serious case reviews / Child Practice Reviews (Wales) repeatedly find: poor information sharing
  • Agencies working in silos
  • Missed signs ("disguised compliance", focus on adult not child)
  • No one speaking to the child
  • Failure to escalate
  • Poor record-keeping
  • "start again syndrome".
Landmark cases
  • Victoria Climbié (2000) → Laming Inquiry → Children Act 2004
  • Peter Connelly ("Baby P", 2007)
  • Daniel Pelka (2012)
  • Arthur Labinjo-Hughes and Star Hobson (2020–21) → national review.
Professional consequencesGMC fitness-to-practise action for failing to act.

los.text: Describe how safeguarding is everyone’s business and professional responsibility
sessions: Case presentation and Introduction to Safeguarding Children
los.html:
"Safeguarding is everyone's business/responsibility"Every professional (and every doctor, regardless of specialty, including adult services) has a duty to recognise and respond to concerns about children (and adults at risk).
Legal/policy basis
  • Children Act 1989 (s47 duty to investigate; welfare paramount) and 2004 (duty to cooperate, safeguard)
  • Social Services and Well-being (Wales) Act 2014 (duty to report a child at risk for relevant partners)
  • Wales Safeguarding Procedures (2019)
  • Working Together (England).
GMC guidance(Protecting children and young people, 2012)
  • All doctors must act on concerns
  • Share information appropriately
  • Keep up to date with training
  • "Think Family" (an adult patient's issues may put a child at risk).
Training levelsLevel 1–3 (Intercollegiate Document); named and designated doctors/nurses for expertise.
Key behaviours
  • Be alert
  • Listen to the child
  • Record accurately
  • Don't investigate yourself
  • Discuss with senior/safeguarding lead
  • Refer to social services/police
  • Share information (consent not required if seeking it increases risk or delays action)
  • Follow up.

los.text: Recall the RCPCH Systematic Review evidence on Child Abuse, NICE Guidance, and identify key evidenced based signs of inflicted injuries and neglect.
sessions: The evidence base for child protection (Part 1 & 2)
los.html:
RCPCH Child Protection Evidence (systematic reviews) and NICE CG89 ("When to suspect child maltreatment"; consider vs suspect).
Bruising(most common injury in physical abuse)
  • Non-mobile infants with any bruise → suspect abuse ("Those who don't cruise rarely bruise").
  • Sites: TEN-4-FACESp (Torso, Ears, Neck, Frenulum, Angle of jaw, Cheeks, Eyelids, Subconjunctiva; any bruise in <4 months; patterned).
  • Clusters, bruises on soft areas (cheeks, buttocks, genitals), petechiae, patterned (hand/fingertip, slap marks, ligature, implement), bite marks. Accidental bruises: bony prominences on front (shins, forehead) in mobile children.
Fractures
  • Rib fractures (esp. posterior: squeezing)
  • Metaphyseal "corner/bucket-handle" fractures
  • Multiple fractures of different ages
  • Femoral fractures in non-ambulant
  • Skull fractures in infants. → skeletal survey in <2 yrs with suspected abuse.
Burns/scalds
  • Immersion scalds with clear tide marks, glove/stocking distribution, sparing of flexures, symmetrical
  • Contact burns with clear shape (cigarette: round 0.5–1 cm), burns on back/buttocks/soles.
Abusive head traumaSubdural haemorrhages, retinal haemorrhages (multilayer), encephalopathy, apnoea; often with no external injury. → CT/MRI head, ophthalmology.
OtherOral injuries (torn frenulum), abdominal injuries, bites, delay in seeking care, history inconsistent/changing/implausible, injury inconsistent with development.
NeglectFaltering growth, poor hygiene, untreated illness/dental caries, missed appointments/immunisations, inappropriate clothing, developmental delay, lack of supervision → injuries, ingestions.
ExcludeBleeding disorders (FBC, clotting), osteogenesis imperfecta, Mongolian blue spots (document at birth).

los.text: Recall risk factors for and indicators of CSA and CSE
sessions: Child sexual assault & Child Sexual Exploitation
los.html:
Child sexual abuse (CSA)Forcing or enticing a child to take part in sexual activities (contact or non-contact, including online).
Child sexual exploitation (CSE)
  • a form of CSA where a child is coerced/manipulated into sexual activity in exchange for something (money, drugs, alcohol, gifts, affection, status) or for the advantage of the perpetrator
  • Often involves grooming (in person or online), may appear consensual to the child.
Risk factors
  • Disability
  • Being looked after/in care
  • Previous abuse
  • Domestic abuse
  • Parental substance misuse/mental illness
  • Going missing
  • School exclusion
  • Isolation
  • LGBTQ+ young people
  • Unsupervised internet use
  • Gang association
  • Learning difficulties.
Indicators
  • Physical: genital/anal injury, bleeding, STIs (gonorrhoea, chlamydia, trichomonas, syphilis, HIV in prepubertal child = strongly suggests abuse), pregnancy (<13), recurrent UTIs/vulvovaginitis (non-specific), soreness.
  • Behavioural: sexualised behaviour inappropriate for age, disclosure, self-harm, eating disorder, low mood, regression (bedwetting), fear of particular people/places, running away.
  • CSE-specific: older boyfriend/girlfriend, unexplained gifts/money/new phone, going missing, staying out late, getting into cars, substance misuse, truancy, repeat STIs/terminations, associating with gangs, change in friends.

los.text: Apply knowledge of the role & nature of the medical assessment in CSA
sessions: Child sexual assault & Child Sexual Exploitation
los.html:
Who
  • Specialist paediatric Sexual Assault Referral Centres (SARCs) (e.g. Swansea "New Pathways"/Paediatric SARC services) with paediatricians + forensic physicians
  • Joint with police/social services after strategy discussion.
  • Not done by non-specialists ("don't examine to 'confirm'").
Purpose
  • Holistic healthcare (not only evidence): assess and treat injuries, STI testing/prophylaxis, emergency contraception, HIV PEP, pregnancy testing, mental health and wellbeing
  • Reassurance for child and family ("body is OK")
  • Forensic evidence collection (time-critical: acute within ~7 days, swabs) and documentation
  • Safeguarding assessment and follow-up.
Nature
  • Child-centred, with consent (child/parent), chaperone, explained at every step
  • May use colposcope for photo-documentation
  • Examination is often normal (genital tissues heal quickly; most CSA leaves no physical signs) → a normal exam does not exclude abuse.
TimingAcute (within 72 h–7 days: urgent for forensic samples and prophylaxis) vs non-acute/historical (planned).
InterviewsFormal ABE (Achieving Best Evidence) interview by police/social worker; clinicians should not conduct investigative interviews; record any spontaneous disclosure verbatim.
Follow-upRepeat STI tests, psychological support (ISVA/ChISVA), therapy, school support.

los.text: Recall safeguarding children guidance and procedure.
sessions: National guidelines & procedures, including more recent developments in SGC
los.html:
• Process (Wales Safeguarding Procedures, Children Act 1989):
1. ConcernDiscuss with senior/safeguarding lead (don't delay in emergencies).
2
  • Referral (duty to report) to local authority children's social services (phone, then written within 24 h, e.g. MARF: Multi-Agency Referral Form)
  • Police if immediate danger/crime.
3Social services decide within 1 working day: no further action / care and support assessment / strategy discussion (social services, police, health) if reasonable cause to suspect significant harm.
4Section 47 enquiry (child protection enquiry) ± medical examination, ABE interview.
5. Initial child protection conference(within 15 working days of strategy discussion)Decides on Child Protection Register/plan (categories below).
6Core group implements plan; review conferences (3 months then every 6 months).
7Court orders if needed: Emergency Protection Order, police protection (72 h), care orders.
Information sharingLawful without consent where necessary to protect (Data Protection Act/GDPR permits); record decisions and rationale.
DocumentationContemporaneous, factual, verbatim quotes, body maps, photographs (with consent), dated/timed/signed.

los.text: Describe what is meant by Fabricated and/or Induced Illness, & Perplexing Presentations. Describe alerting signs.
sessions: National guidelines & procedures, including more recent developments in SGC
los.html:
Fabricated or induced illness (FII)
  • a carer (usually mother) fabricates, exaggerates or induces symptoms/signs in a child, causing harm (unnecessary investigations/treatment, restricted life, physical harm).
  • Formerly "Münchausen syndrome by proxy".
  • Motivation not required for diagnosis.
Perplexing presentations (RCPCH 2021)
  • Alerting signs present but no likely physical harm yet
  • The earlier stage requiring a structured approach (one responsible paediatrician, health chronology, "Health and Education Rehabilitation Plan").
Alerting signs
  • Reported symptoms/signs not observed independently (only when carer present), not explained by any medical condition, or inconsistent with investigation results.
  • High number of presentations, doctor shopping, multiple specialists, requests for second opinions, insisting on more investigations.
  • Unusual or unexplained biochemical results (e.g. hypoglycaemia with high insulin and low C-peptide: exogenous insulin; poisoning; salt), unusual infections in lines (contamination), blood in samples not from child.
  • Treatment response unexpectedly poor; symptoms recur when child returns home; new symptoms as old ones resolve.
  • Child's daily life restricted beyond what disease would explain (wheelchair, school non-attendance, special diets, feeding tubes).
  • Carer seems unusually knowledgeable/medically involved; history of carer's own unexplained illnesses.
Response
  • Discuss with named doctor/safeguarding team
  • Establish a single coordinating clinician
  • Consolidate records
  • Avoid confronting parent prematurely if risk of escalation
  • Refer to social services if likely significant harm
  • Covert surveillance only by police.

los.text: Apply the Mental Capacity Act for medical practice to ethical scenarios
sessions: MHS: Consent for adults lacking capacity and Children
los.html:
Mental Capacity Act 2005(England and Wales; age 16+)
  • 5 principles: (1) presume capacity; (2) take all practicable steps to support decision-making; (3) unwise decisions don't mean lack of capacity; (4) decisions for someone lacking capacity must be in their best interests; (5) choose the least restrictive option.
  • Two-stage test: is there an impairment/disturbance of mind or brain? Does it mean the person cannot (functional test): understand relevant information, retain it, use/weigh it, communicate a decision. Decision- and time-specific.
  • Best interests checklist: consider person's past and present wishes, feelings, beliefs and values; consult family/carers/LPA/attorney; consider whether capacity may be regained (delay if possible); don't base on age/appearance/condition; not motivated by desire to bring about death.
  • Advance decisions to refuse treatment (ADRT) (life-sustaining: written, signed, witnessed, "even if life at risk"), Lasting Power of Attorney (health and welfare), IMCA if no one to consult (serious medical treatment), Court of Protection, DoLS (being replaced by Liberty Protection Safeguards).
Children
  • Under 16 → Gillick competence (sufficient understanding and intelligence)
  • 16–17 presumed capable (Family Law Reform Act 1969) but refusal of life-saving treatment can be overridden by court/person with parental responsibility in the child's best interests
  • Those with parental responsibility consent if child lacks competence.
Scenarios
  • Emergency treatment without consent (doctrine of necessity)
  • Jehovah's Witness adult refusing blood (valid refusal) vs child (court can authorise)
  • Patient with delirium refusing treatment
  • Fluctuating capacity.

los.text: Describe child trafficking and slavery in the UK.
sessions: Human slavery, modern trafficking, child sexual assault
los.html:
Child trafficking
  • Recruitment
  • Transportation
  • Transfer
  • Harbouring or receipt of a child for the purpose of exploitation (no need for force/deception for children: a child cannot consent).
  • Can be within the UK (internal trafficking, e.g. "county lines") or international.
Modern slavery(Modern Slavery Act 2015)Slavery, servitude, forced or compulsory labour, and human trafficking.
Forms of exploitation
  • Sexual exploitation
  • Criminal exploitation (county lines drug running, cannabis farms, pickpocketing)
  • Labour exploitation (nail bars, car washes, agriculture)
  • Domestic servitude
  • Forced marriage
  • Benefit fraud
  • Organ harvesting
  • Illegal adoption.
UK picture
  • Children make up a large proportion of National Referral Mechanism (NRM) referrals
  • Most commonly UK nationals (criminal exploitation/county lines), plus Albanian, Vietnamese, Eritrean, Sudanese children
  • Unaccompanied asylum-seeking children at high risk.
Systems
  • NRM (formal identification and support; consent not needed for under-18s), Independent Child Trafficking Guardians, Modern Slavery Helpline, police, social services
  • Victims shouldn't be criminalised (statutory defence).

los.text: Describe signs and symptoms of child slavery and trafficking.
sessions: Human slavery, modern trafficking, child sexual assault
los.html:
Signs and symptoms
  • Accompanied by unrelated adult who controls, speaks for them, holds their ID/passport; inconsistent explanations of relationship.
  • No documents, false documents, unclear immigration status; doesn't know address; recently moved.
  • Untreated injuries/illnesses, delayed presentation, signs of physical/sexual abuse, STIs, pregnancy, malnutrition, poor dental health, fatigue, occupational injuries (chemical burns, cuts).
  • Psychological: fear, anxiety, withdrawn, PTSD, scripted or rehearsed account, distrust of authorities, fear of deportation, loyalty to exploiters.
  • Not in school, working long hours, unexplained money/phones/clothes, going missing, travelling to other towns (county lines), found in cannabis farms, substance misuse, gang tattoos/branding.
  • Living in poor or overcrowded conditions at the workplace.
Response
  • See the child alone (with professional interpreter, not companion)
  • Safety first
  • Don't alert the controller
  • Document
  • Refer to social services and police
  • NRM referral
  • Safeguarding lead
  • Ensure health needs are met.

los.text: Apply literature review skills in relation to specific healthcare issues
sessions: MHS: Critical Appraisal 1: case control and cohort studies
los.html:
Critical appraisalSystematically assessing research for validity, results and relevance to a specific question.
Literature review skills
  • PICO question → search strategy (keywords, MeSH, Boolean AND/OR/NOT, truncation, filters) across PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, PsycINFO, Cochrane Library
  • Inclusion/exclusion criteria
  • Record search (PRISMA flow)
  • Manage references.
Case–control studies
  • Start with outcome (cases with disease vs controls without) → look back at exposure.
  • Good for rare diseases, quick, cheap.
  • Measure: odds ratio.
  • Problems: recall bias, selection bias (choice of controls), confounding
  • Can't calculate incidence.
Cohort studies
  • Start with exposure → follow up for outcome (prospective or retrospective).
  • Good for rare exposures, multiple outcomes, temporal sequence, incidence, relative risk.
  • Problems: expensive/slow (prospective), loss to follow-up (attrition bias), confounding.
Appraisal checklists
  • CASP, CEBM
  • For observational: STROBE reporting, Newcastle–Ottawa quality scale.
  • Questions: clear question? appropriate design? recruitment acceptable? exposure/outcome accurately measured? confounders identified/adjusted? follow-up complete/long enough? precision (CIs)? applicable locally? fits with other evidence? (Bradford Hill).
Confounding controlled by matching, restriction, stratification, multivariable regression.

los.text: Discuss factors which make a child vulnerable.
sessions: Vulnerable children and their families
los.html:
Child factors
  • Age (infants <1 yr most at risk of serious/fatal abuse)
  • Disability/complex health needs
  • Prematurity
  • Behavioural difficulties
  • Being looked after/care leaver
  • Young carer
  • Unaccompanied asylum-seeking child
  • LGBTQ+
  • Chronic illness
  • Not attending school.
Parent/carer factors("toxic trio")
  • Domestic abuse, parental mental illness, parental substance/alcohol misuse.
  • Also: parental learning disability, young parents, parents abused as children, criminality, unrelated adult in household, history of violence, previous children removed.
Family/environmentalPoverty, poor housing/overcrowding, homelessness, social isolation, unemployment, debt, frequent moves, community violence, gang activity.
OtherOnline risks, extremism/radicalisation (Prevent), FGM, forced marriage, trafficking.
Protective factorsSecure attachment to a caring adult, supportive extended family, good school engagement, community support, early help.
ApproachThink Family, early help/family support before crisis, holistic assessment of needs.

los.text: Discuss the role of health and other multiagency professionals in the safeguarding process
sessions: Clinical forum - working together
los.html:
• Multi-agency safeguarding: no single agency has the full picture → information sharing is critical.
AgencyRole
Children's social servicesLead agency: receive referrals, assessments, s47 enquiries, chair strategy discussions/conferences, care plans, court applications
PoliceInvestigate crime, protect children (police protection powers), joint investigation, ABE interviews, PPN/MASH
Health (GPs, health visitors, school nurses, midwives, paediatricians, ED, CAMHS, adult services)Recognise and refer, medical assessment, share health information, attend conferences, support plans; named/designated professionals provide advice
Education (schools, designated safeguarding leads)Daily contact, recognise changes, refer, Operation Encompass (domestic abuse notifications)
OthersProbation, housing, voluntary sector (NSPCC), CAFCASS (courts), youth services
StructuresMASH (multi-agency safeguarding hubs), Regional Safeguarding Children Boards (Wales), MARAC (domestic abuse), MAPPA (offenders), Child Practice Reviews.
Health visitorUniversal service (Healthy Child Wales Programme), home visits, often first to notice neglect.

los.text: Perform a breast examination, following clinical and ethical guidelines.
sessions: Breast Examination
los.html:
Prepare
  • Introduce
  • Explain purpose and that it's an intimate examination
  • Valid consent
  • Offer chaperone (document name or refusal)
  • Privacy
  • Exposure only as needed (to waist)
  • Ask about pain/symptoms (lump, nipple discharge, skin change, pain, FHx).
Inspection(patient sitting at 45° or upright)
  • Hands on hips/pressing (pectoral contraction), hands behind head/raised, leaning forward (pendulous breasts).
  • Look for asymmetry, skin changes (peau d'orange, dimpling/tethering, erythema, ulceration), nipple changes (inversion, retraction, discharge, eczema = Paget's), visible lumps, scars.
Palpation(patient lying at 45°, hand behind head on side examined)
  • Start with normal side
  • Use flat of fingers, systematic (clock-face/concentric circles or vertical strips) covering all quadrants, axillary tail, retroareolar area
  • Nipple (ask patient to express discharge).
Lump characteristicsSite (quadrant, distance from nipple), size, shape, consistency, surface, mobility/tethering (to skin or muscle: contract pectoralis), tenderness, overlying skin, fluctuance, transillumination.
Lymph nodesAxillary (support arm; apical, anterior, posterior, central, lateral groups), supraclavicular and infraclavicular, cervical.
CompleteCover patient, thank, wash hands; offer further examination (abdominal for hepatomegaly, spine for bony tenderness, chest).

los.text: Present clinical findings from a breast examination using appropriate medical terminology and structure.
sessions: Breast Examination
los.html:
Structure"I examined [name], a [age]-year-old woman, with a chaperone present (name)."
Inspection"On inspection the breasts were symmetrical with no visible masses, skin changes or nipple abnormalities in all positions" (or describe abnormality).
PalpationDescribe any lump with this checklist:
FeatureSay
Size"[x] cm"
Consistency, surfaceHard/firm/rubbery; irregular/smooth
SiteQuadrant (e.g. upper outer), side, distance from nipple, clock position
MobilityMobile/fixed; tethered or not to skin/underlying muscle
OtherTenderness, overlying skin changes
NippleDischarge (colour, single/multiple ducts, bloody).
Nodes"No palpable axillary, supraclavicular or cervical lymphadenopathy" (or describe).
Summary + impressione.g. "These findings are suspicious for breast carcinoma. I would refer urgently for triple assessment."
Triple assessmentClinical exam + imaging (mammogram ± USS; USS only if <35) + core biopsy.
TerminologyUse quadrants (UOQ, UIQ, LOQ, LIQ), clock-face position, retroareolar, axillary tail; peau d'orange, tethering, fixation.

los.text: Identify and explain the risk factors that contribute to a child’s vulnerability, including social, familial, and medical aspects.
sessions: Recognition of and risk factors for Non-Accidental Injury
los.html:
ChildAge (<1), disability, prematurity/low birthweight, chronic illness, behavioural problems, unwanted/difficult pregnancy, separation from parents at birth (NICU), looked-after status.
Familial
  • Domestic abuse, parental mental illness, substance misuse ("toxic trio")
  • Young/isolated parents
  • Unrelated male in household
  • Parental history of abuse in childhood
  • Previous child protection involvement/children removed
  • Family conflict
  • Unrealistic expectations of child
  • Harsh discipline
  • Criminality.
SocialPoverty, unemployment, poor/overcrowded housing, homelessness, social isolation, frequent moves, lack of support network, community violence, immigration insecurity.
Medical/health careMissed appointments/immunisations, delayed presentation, frequent ED attendance, failure to follow medical advice, carer's own health problems.
Explain
  • Risk factors increase likelihood but don't prove abuse
  • Most families with risk factors don't abuse
  • Abuse occurs in all social classes.
  • Use to guide early help and vigilance.

los.text: Recognise and interpret key signs and symptoms indicative of child abuse or neglect and consider them in clinical assessment
sessions: Recognition of and risk factors for Non-Accidental Injury
los.html:
See LO 3 (signs of physical abuse) and LO 4 (sexual abuse).
Emotional abuse
  • Persistent emotional ill-treatment (rejection, humiliation, threats, witnessing domestic abuse, age-inappropriate expectations, overprotection) → low self-esteem
  • Anxiety
  • Developmental delay
  • Frozen watchfulness
  • Attachment problems
  • Self-harm.
Neglect
  • Faltering growth (gains weight in hospital)
  • Poor hygiene
  • Inappropriate clothing
  • Untreated medical/dental problems
  • Missed appointments
  • Repeated accidents (poor supervision)
  • Developmental delay
  • Hunger/stealing food
  • Frequent unexplained school absence.
Red flags in clinical assessment
  • History: no explanation, vague, inconsistent between carers or over time, inconsistent with injury/development, delay in presentation, child's account differs, blaming siblings.
  • Examination: injury pattern (TEN-4-FACESp bruises, burns, fractures), multiple injuries of different ages, signs of neglect, interaction (fearful child, inappropriate parental response).
  • Behaviour: withdrawn, aggressive, sexualised, regression, self-harm, running away.
Clinical action
  • Full examination (body map)
  • Growth
  • Investigations in suspected physical abuse (FBC/clotting, skeletal survey in <2 yrs, CT head in <1 yr; ophthalmology)
  • Consider medical differentials
  • Document
  • Discuss with senior/safeguarding team
  • Refer.

los.text: Analyse the physical, psychological, and social indicators to construct a holistic understanding of potential child abuse cases.
sessions: Think Adult Think Child: Safeguarding the hidden Child exercise”: Recognition and response to emerging safeguarding concerns of a child where the child is not the primary patient.
los.html:
"Think Adult, Think Child" / "Think Family"When treating an adult, consider the children in their care or household (the "hidden child").
TriggersAdult with mental illness, substance misuse, domestic abuse, overdose or alcohol-related injury.
Holistic analysis
  • Physical: injuries, neglect, growth, health care access.
  • Psychological: child's emotional state, behaviour, attachment, being a young carer, exposure to violence or parental distress.
  • Social: household members, housing, poverty, school attendance, support network, who is looking after the child now.
Questions to ask adult patients"Do you have children or care for any? Who is looking after them now? Are they safe? Do they live with you?" Also pregnancy.
AssessParenting capacity, impact of adult's condition on child, protective factors, immediate safety (e.g. parent admitted after overdose, child home alone), long-term needs.
ActShare concerns with safeguarding team/social services, record children's details, liaise with GP/health visitor/school nurse, early help referral.

los.text: Identify and interpret red flags and risk factors for child abuse from carers’ histories, behaviours, and presentations.
sessions: Think Adult Think Child: Safeguarding the hidden Child exercise”: Recognition and response to emerging safeguarding concerns of a child where the child is not the primary patient.
los.html:
Red flags in carers' history
  • Inconsistent or changing account
  • Explanation doesn't fit injury/child's development
  • Delay in seeking help
  • No explanation offered
  • Blaming the child/sibling
  • Vague about events
  • Hostility or evasiveness
  • Refusing examination/investigation
  • Multiple ED attendances/different hospitals
  • Previous unexplained injuries
  • History of domestic abuse/substance misuse/mental illness
  • Previous child protection involvement.
Behaviours
  • Lack of concern or excessive anger
  • Inappropriate responses to child's distress
  • Controlling
  • Overly critical or rejecting
  • Rough handling
  • Leaving child unsupervised
  • Under the influence of alcohol/drugs
  • Disguised compliance (appearing cooperative without change)
  • Not engaging with services
  • Unrealistic expectations.
PresentationsInjuries in non-mobile infants, recurrent "accidents", ingestions, FII alerting signs, faltering growth, unexplained symptoms, missed appointments, late antenatal booking/concealed pregnancy.
Interpret
  • Consider in context (cultural practices, medical conditions), but don't let explanations of "parental stress" override the child's welfare
  • Child's perspective first.

los.text: Evaluate the roles and responsibilities of health and other professionals in the safeguarding process, and explain the importance of collaborative, multi-agency working to build a complete safeguarding picture.
sessions: Think Adult Think Child: Safeguarding the hidden Child exercise”: Recognition and response to emerging safeguarding concerns of a child where the child is not the primary patient.
los.html:
Health professionals
  • Recognise and refer
  • Assess and treat
  • Provide medical opinion (paediatrician)
  • Share information
  • Contribute to assessments
  • Attend strategy meetings and conferences
  • Participate in core group plans
  • Document
  • Follow up
  • Named/designated professionals advise and support.
Other professionalsSocial workers (lead, assessments, plans), police (investigation, protection), teachers/designated safeguarding leads, health visitors/school nurses, probation, housing, third sector.
Importance of collaborative, multi-agency working
  • Each agency holds pieces of the jigsaw; abuse often only becomes clear when information is combined (lessons from serious case reviews).
  • Shared thresholds and language, clear roles, timely information sharing, joint decision-making, coordinated plans, avoids duplication and missed signs.
  • Challenges: different priorities/cultures, confidentiality concerns, workload, poor communication, professional hierarchy (escalate if disagree: "professional challenge/escalation" policies).
Principle"The child's welfare is paramount"; information sharing to protect a child is justified even without consent.

los.text: Explain the potential outcomes of safeguarding assessments, including Child Protection Registration and its categories, and apply this knowledge to decision-making in clinical practice.
sessions: Think Adult Think Child: Safeguarding the hidden Child exercise”: Recognition and response to emerging safeguarding concerns of a child where the child is not the primary patient.
los.html:
Possible outcomes after referral/assessment
  • No further action
  • Advice/early help (family support)
  • Care and support plan (child in need of care and support)
  • Strategy discussion → s47 enquiry
  • Child protection conference → Child Protection Register (Wales) / child protection plan (England)
  • Legal proceedings (care orders, supervision orders, emergency protection orders, placement in care).
Child Protection Register categories (Wales)
  • Physical abuse, emotional abuse, sexual abuse, neglect (a child may be registered under more than one category).
  • (Financial abuse is relevant to adults, not used for children.)
Child protection planLead social worker (key worker), core group (family + professionals), specific actions and timescales, review conferences; de-registration when risk reduced.
Clinical decision-making applications
  • Know the child's status (check records/flags; Child Protection Information Sharing system) → affects discharge planning, information sharing, who can visit.
  • Inform the key social worker of new concerns, attendances or missed appointments.
  • Don't discharge a child with unresolved concerns until a safe plan exists.
  • Contribute medical reports to conferences/court.
